title: What is the difference between SAST, DAST, IAST, and SCA, and where does each run in the SDLC?
shortTitle: The difference between SAST, DAST, IAST, and SCA — and where each runs in the SDLC

s1_definition.profdef: These are four complementary application-security testing techniques. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes your source or bytecode without running it, finding code-level flaws early in the build. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests the running application from the outside like an attacker, finding runtime and configuration flaws in a deployed environment. IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) instruments the running application with an agent so it observes code execution during functional tests, combining code-level insight with runtime context. SCA (Software Composition Analysis) inventories your third-party and open-source dependencies and flags known vulnerabilities and license risks. Each runs at a different point: SAST and SCA in the build, IAST during integration testing, DAST against a deployed environment.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine securing a new bank branch. SAST is an architect reviewing the blueprints and wiring diagrams for mistakes before anything is switched on. SCA is checking that every pre-made part you bought — locks, alarms, safes from other suppliers — has no known recall or defect. IAST is a trained observer who shadows the staff during a normal business-day rehearsal, watching exactly how each transaction flows and flagging unsafe steps as they happen. DAST is a hired burglar who tries to break into the finished, operating branch from the outside to see what actually gives way.
s1_definition.oneliner: SAST reads your code, SCA checks your dependencies, IAST watches your code run from the inside during tests, and DAST attacks your running app from the outside — each catching a different class of flaw at a different SDLC stage.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** These are four complementary application-security testing techniques. SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes your source or bytecode without running it, finding code-level flaws early in the build. DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests the running application from the outside like an attacker, finding runtime and configuration flaws in a deployed environment. IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing) instruments the running application with an agent so it observes code execution during functional tests, combining code-level insight with runtime context. SCA (Software Composition Analysis) inventories your third-party and open-source dependencies and flags known vulnerabilities and license risks. Each runs at a different point: SAST and SCA in the build, IAST during integration testing, DAST against a deployed environment.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine securing a new bank branch. SAST is an architect reviewing the blueprints and wiring diagrams for mistakes before anything is switched on. SCA is checking that every pre-made part you bought — locks, alarms, safes from other suppliers — has no known recall or defect. IAST is a trained observer who shadows the staff during a normal business-day rehearsal, watching exactly how each transaction flows and flagging unsafe steps as they happen. DAST is a hired burglar who tries to break into the finished, operating branch from the outside to see what actually gives way.

**One line to remember:** SAST reads your code, SCA checks your dependencies, IAST watches your code run from the inside during tests, and DAST attacks your running app from the outside — each catching a different class of flaw at a different SDLC stage.

sections.s2_technical:
SAST, static analysis, examines source code, bytecode, or binaries without executing them. It parses the code into an abstract representation and traces how untrusted data flows through it, flagging patterns like SQL built by string concatenation, missing output encoding, hardcoded secrets, or unsafe deserialization. Its great strength is that it runs early, on every commit, and points at the exact file and line, so fixes are cheap. Its weakness is false positives, because it cannot always tell whether a flagged path is actually reachable or exploitable, and it cannot see configuration or runtime behaviour. It runs in the build or even in the IDE.

DAST, dynamic analysis, tests the application while it is running, usually against a deployed staging environment, by sending crafted requests the way an external attacker would — probing for injection, broken authentication, misconfigured headers, and the like. Its strength is that it finds real, runtime-exposed issues including deployment and configuration problems that static analysis cannot see, and it has very few false positives because it actually triggers the behaviour. Its weaknesses are that it runs late, needs a running environment, only covers paths it manages to reach, and does not point at a specific line of code. It runs in a test or pre-production environment.

IAST sits between the two. It deploys an agent inside the running application so that, while functional or integration tests exercise the app, the agent observes the actual code paths, data flow, and library calls from the inside. Because it sees both the executing code and the live request context, it combines SAST-like precision about where the flaw is with DAST-like confidence that it is real, producing fewer false positives and pinpointing the vulnerable code. Its cost is the runtime overhead of the agent and the need for good test coverage to exercise the paths. It runs during integration and functional testing.

SCA, software composition analysis, is about the code you did not write. Modern applications are mostly third-party and open-source libraries, and most real-world vulnerabilities enter through them. SCA builds an inventory of every direct and transitive dependency, matches it against vulnerability databases such as the National Vulnerability Database, and flags components with known issues, often also checking open-source license compliance. Its strength is catching things like the Log4Shell class of vulnerability the moment a known-bad version is pulled in. It runs in the build, on every commit, and continuously afterward because new vulnerabilities are disclosed against libraries you already shipped.

The senior point is that these are complementary, not competing. SAST and SCA shift security left into the build for fast, cheap, per-commit feedback on your code and your dependencies. IAST adds precision during testing. DAST validates the real running system from the outside. A mature program runs all four at their appropriate stages, because each catches a class of flaw the others miss, and relying on only one leaves a blind spot.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's loan-origination service has a SQL query built by string concatenation, a vulnerable logging library pulled in transitively, and a misconfigured security header that only appears when the app is deployed. No single tool finds all three. This is exactly why SAST, SCA, and DAST are complementary.

Problem 2 — The team wants to know, for each finding, which tool should catch it and at which SDLC stage, so they can place the right check at the right point. This is the where-each-runs question.

Our mini-project is a runnable scan-router simulator: it takes a set of findings, routes each to the technique that detects it, reports the SDLC stage that technique runs at, and confirms full coverage only when all four techniques are present. Classes are `AppSecScanDemo` (driver), `ScanTechnique` (SAST, DAST, IAST, or SCA with its SDLC stage and what it detects), and `Finding` (a vulnerability with the technique expected to catch it).
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
appsec-techniques-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── .github/workflows/security.yml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/com/bank/appsec/
            ├── AppSecScanDemo.java   (main + demo classes)
            └── ScanTechnique.java
```

Configuration (each technique wired into its SDLC stage):

```yaml
# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: appsec
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build-stage:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: SAST (our source, build stage)
        run: semgrep ci --config auto
      - name: SCA (dependencies, build stage)
        run: mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
      - name: Build + IAST-instrumented integration tests
        run: mvn verify -Dcontrast.agent=on   # IAST agent during tests
  deploy-stage:
    needs: build-stage
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to staging
        run: ./deploy-staging.sh
      - name: DAST (running app, pre-prod stage)
        run: zap-baseline.py -t https://staging.nbi.internal/loans
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn -q clean package

# Run the router — see which technique catches which finding, and at what stage
java -cp target/appsec-techniques-demo-1.0.0.jar \
     com.bank.appsec.AppSecScanDemo

# In a real repo the techniques run automatically in security.yml:
#   SAST (semgrep) + SCA (dependency-check) at build,
#   IAST agent during `mvn verify`, DAST (OWASP ZAP) against staging
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three real findings in the loan-origination service — a concatenated SQL query, a vulnerable transitive Log4j dependency, and a missing security header in production config — plus the four techniques with their SDLC stages.

Step 1. The four techniques are defined, each carrying its name, the SDLC stage where it runs, and the class of flaw it detects. SAST and SCA are tagged to the build stage, IAST to integration testing, and DAST to a deployed staging environment.

Step 2. The first finding, the concatenated SQL in the repository, is a code-level flaw in the bank's own source. It is routed to SAST, and the demo logs that SAST catches it at the build stage because it reads the source and traces untrusted data into the query.

Step 3. The second finding, the vulnerable transitive Log4j, is not in the bank's code at all — it is a dependency. It is routed to SCA, and the demo logs that SCA catches it at the build stage by matching the dependency inventory against vulnerability databases, the only technique that reliably finds a known-bad library.

Step 4. The third finding, the missing Strict-Transport-Security header, only exists in the deployed configuration and is invisible to source analysis. It is routed to DAST, and the demo logs that DAST catches it against staging by probing the running app's responses from the outside.

Step 5. IAST is noted as running during integration tests with an agent inside the app, giving precise, low-false-positive findings on the code paths the tests exercise — complementing the other three rather than replacing them.

Step 6. The final log states that full coverage exists only because all four techniques are present at their proper stages; dropping any one would leave a specific finding undetected, which is the whole point of using them together.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SDLC timeline (left → right)   Code → Build → Test → Deploy/Staging → Prod
    │
    ├─ SAST  ──runs at Build──→ reads SOURCE (no run)   → SQLi, secrets, line-precise
    │                                                     (some false positives)
    ├─ SCA   ──runs at Build + continuously──→ scans DEPENDENCIES
    │                                            → known-vulnerable libs (Log4Shell)
    ├─ IAST  ──runs during Test──→ AGENT inside running app during functional tests
    │                               → precise code path + real context (low FP)
    └─ DAST  ──runs at Staging──→ attacks RUNNING app from OUTSIDE
                                    → config/header/auth flaws (very low FP, no line)

  Finding 1 (concatenated SQL)   ─→ SAST
  Finding 2 (vulnerable Log4j)   ─→ SCA
  Finding 3 (missing HSTS header)─→ DAST
  (IAST would catch e.g. a tainted-input flow exercised by an integration test)

  All four together = full coverage; any one alone = blind spots
```

```
  ── State Diagram: where a flaw is caught ───────────────────

  [flaw in our code]   → SAST (build)  → fixed early
  [flaw in dependency] → SCA (build)   → upgrade/patch

  [flaw in running/config] → DAST (staging) → fix config
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
SAST, DAST, IAST, and SCA are four complementary application-security testing techniques, each catching a different class of flaw at a different point in the lifecycle. SAST, static analysis, reads your source or bytecode without running it and traces how untrusted data flows through the code, so it catches things like SQL built by string concatenation, hardcoded secrets, and unsafe deserialization early, on every commit, and points at the exact line; its trade-off is false positives because it cannot always tell whether a path is truly reachable. DAST, dynamic analysis, tests the running application from the outside like an attacker against a deployed environment, so it finds runtime and configuration flaws such as missing security headers, broken authentication, and injection that static analysis cannot see, with very few false positives because it actually triggers the behaviour, but it runs late and does not point at a line.

IAST sits between them: it instruments the running application with an agent so that while your functional and integration tests exercise the app, the agent observes the real code paths, data flow, and library calls from the inside. That combination gives SAST-like precision about where the flaw is with DAST-like confidence that it is real, so it produces few false positives, at the cost of agent overhead and needing good test coverage. SCA, software composition analysis, is about the code you did not write — it inventories every direct and transitive dependency, matches it against vulnerability databases, and flags known-vulnerable libraries and license risks, which matters enormously because most real-world vulnerabilities enter through dependencies, as Log4Shell showed; it runs in the build and continuously afterward because new vulnerabilities are disclosed against libraries you already shipped.

Where each runs follows from what it needs: SAST and SCA shift left into the build for fast per-commit feedback on your code and your dependencies, IAST runs during integration testing, and DAST runs against a deployed staging environment, with continuous SCA extending into production. At National Bank of India our loan-origination service had a concatenated SQL query, a vulnerable transitive logging library, and a misconfigured security header that only appeared once deployed, and no single tool found all three — SAST caught the SQL, SCA caught the library, and DAST caught the header. That is exactly why I treat them as a layered set rather than a choice; relying on only one leaves a predictable blind spot.
